photons-s1.title: Emission lines of a gas discharge tube
photons-s1.text: A student views the light from a tube of hot hydrogen gas through a spectroscope and records four bright lines in the visible region.

photons-s2.title: Photon energy and wavelength
photons-s2.text: The energy of one photon calculated for several wavelengths of light.

items.q: What is the frequency of line A?

mistakes.why: Value: you used the wavelength in nm. Convert to meters first: 656.3 nm = 6.563 × 10⁻⁷ m.
Value: you divided λ by c. Frequency is ν = c/λ.

items.q: What is the energy of one photon of line A?

options: Right: E = hc/λ with λ in meters.
This is hλ. Energy is E = hν = hc/λ, which falls as λ rises.
This is the energy of a mole of photons; one photon is 6.022 × 10²³ times smaller.
This used λ in nm. Convert first: 656.3 nm = 6.563 × 10⁻⁷ m.

items.q: Which line comes from the largest drop in energy between two levels?

why.correct: E = hc/λ, so the shortest wavelength carries the most energy. Line D, at 410.2 nm, comes from the largest energy drop.
options: Right: shortest wavelength, most energy.
Line A has the longest wavelength, so the smallest energy drop of the four.
Line B, at 486.1 nm, is a longer wavelength than two of the other lines.
Line C, at 434.0 nm, is longer than the 410.2 nm line.

items.q: Why does hydrogen emit only these particular wavelengths rather than a continuous rainbow?
options: Its electron energies are quantized, so only photons matching the gaps between levels are emitted.
Its electrons can sit at any energy, but the spectroscope filters out the other wavelengths.
Hydrogen atoms are too small to emit light of any other color than these four.
Hot hydrogen gas reflects these four colors from the light in the room.

why.correct: Electrons in an atom occupy fixed levels. A drop from one level to another emits a photon whose energy, and so wavelength, equals that gap exactly. A few gaps give a few lines.
options: Right: fixed levels, fixed photon energies.
A spectroscope spreads light out; it would show a continuous spectrum if one were emitted.
Atom size does not pick the colors; the gaps between levels do.
The light is emitted by the hot gas, not reflected.

items.q: What is the energy of one mole of line D photons, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Value: that is one photon. Multiply by Avogadro's number for a mole of photons.

items.q: Which relationship does the graph show?
options: Energy per photon is inversely proportional to wavelength.
Energy per photon is directly proportional to wavelength.
Energy per photon falls by the same amount for each 100 nm.
Energy per photon does not depend on wavelength.

why.correct: Doubling the wavelength from 300 nm to 600 nm halves the energy, from 6.62 to 3.31 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. E = hc/λ.
options: Right: E × λ is constant.
Energy falls as wavelength rises.
The drop gets smaller at longer wavelengths, so it is not linear.
The curve changes by a factor of four across the graph.

items.q: By what factor is the energy of a 250 nm photon greater than that of a 750 nm photon?

mistakes.why: Value: you inverted the ratio. The shorter wavelength has the greater energy.

why.correct: E is proportional to 1/λ, so E(250)/E(750) = 750/250 = 3. No constants are needed.

items.q: An electronic transition in a molecule requires 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Which wavelength of light could cause it?
options: About 400 nm
About 200 nm
About 600 nm
About 800 nm

why.correct: λ = hc/E = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 2.998 × 10⁸) / 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 400 nm. The graph shows 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J at about 400 nm.
options: Right: the photon energy matches the gap.
A 200 nm photon carries about twice the energy needed.
A 600 nm photon carries only about two thirds of the energy needed.
An 800 nm photon carries about half the energy needed.

items.q: A student says that a very bright red lamp (700 nm) can cause the transition in the previous question if it is bright enough. Which response is best?
options: No: each red photon has about 2.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, less than the gap, and brighter light only adds more such photons.
Yes: a brighter lamp has more energy in total, so it is able to supply the 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J needed.
Yes: bright light has a shorter wavelength than dim light, so it carries more energy per photon.
No: red light has more energy per photon than the gap, so it passes through without being absorbed.

why.correct: A transition is caused by one photon of matching energy. A 700 nm photon carries hc/λ = 2.84 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Brightness changes the number of photons, not the energy of each.
options: Right: energy per photon decides.
Total energy is not what matters; each photon must match the gap.
Brightness does not change wavelength.
Red photons have less energy than the gap, not more.

items.q: A microwave oven uses radiation with a frequency of 2.45 × 10⁹ s⁻¹. What is its wavelength, in meters?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided ν by c. Wavelength is λ = c/ν.
Value: you multiplied c by ν. Wavelength is λ = c/ν.

items.q: Sodium street lamps emit yellow light at 589 nm. What is the energy of one photon of this light?

options: Right: E = hc/λ with λ in meters.
This used λ in nm. Convert first: 589 nm = 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ m.
This is hλ. Energy is E = hc/λ.
This is a mole of photons, not one photon.

items.q: What is the energy of one mole of 589 nm photons, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Units: that is J/mol. Divide by 1000 to give kJ/mol.
Value: you used 589 nm as if it were meters. Convert: 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ m.

why.correct: E(one photon) = hc/λ = 3.3726 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Per mole: × 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 2.0310 × 10⁵ J/mol = 203.1 kJ/mol, which is 203 kJ/mol.

items.q: Which equation gives the energy of one photon from its frequency?
options: E = hν
E = hλ
E = mc²
c = λν

why.correct: The energy of a photon is Planck's constant times its frequency.
options: Right: Planck's constant times frequency.
Energy falls as wavelength rises, so E is not proportional to λ.
That relates mass and energy; it is not on the equations sheet for this course.
This links wavelength and frequency, not energy.

items.q: When the wavelength of light is doubled, what happens to its frequency and to the energy of each photon?
options: Both are halved.
Both are doubled.
Frequency halves; energy doubles.
Frequency doubles; energy halves.

why.correct: c = λν with c fixed, so doubling λ halves ν. E = hν, so the energy halves too.
options: Right: c fixed, E ∝ ν.
Longer waves have lower frequency and less energy.
E is proportional to ν, so they change together.
Doubling λ lowers ν, not raises it.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the energy of one mole of photons from a wavelength in nm in order.
options: Convert the wavelength from nm to m
Calculate the frequency, ν = c/λ
Calculate the energy of one photon, E = hν
Multiply by Avogadro's number
Divide by 1000 to give kJ/mol

why.correct: Units first, then frequency, then energy per photon, then per mole, then kJ.

items.q: An atom has two levels 3.03 × 10⁻¹⁹ J apart. Which photons could it absorb to move an electron between exactly these two levels? Select all that apply.
options: 656 nm
486 nm
328 nm

why.correct: λ = hc/E = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 2.998 × 10⁸) / 3.03 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.56 × 10⁻⁷ m = 656 nm. Only a photon of that energy matches the gap; photons of other energies are not absorbed for this transition.
options: Right: its energy equals the gap.
A 486 nm photon carries 4.09 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, more than the gap.
A 1,312 nm photon carries half the energy needed.
A 328 nm photon carries twice the energy needed.
